titulo: My Grandmother Walked Every Day Until 98 — The 5-Minute Japanese Morning Routine for Weak Legs

eventos.t: On the first morning with my Tuesday class, I had twelve women in my living room. The oldest was Mrs. Sato, seventy-nine, and she brought her own cushion. She could not lift her arms past her ears that first day, because of a bad shoulder from years of carrying laundry up the stairs. In the third week, she lifted them all the way, and she laughed and almost fell back in her chair. Nobody is fast a

And a small thing you will notice: your hands go down. When the shoulders loosen, the hands hang beside the chair instead of climbing up to the ears. Stand in front of a mirror if you have one. That is the whole test — where are my hands?

Why it matters: the neck, the tops of the shoulders, the inside of the shoulder blades.

A kitchen chair. Five minutes. Before your tea gets cold.

If you forget everything I said today, keep two words: slow, and together. Slow is strong, because a slow movement lets the body answer you. Together is kind, because you do not have to do all five on the first morning. One is enough. One movement, ten times, in your nightgown, before the tea. Then tomorrow, two.
